blocks.text: GIS stands for geographic information system: a digital map with data behind it. Click a property and you can pull up its zoning, lot dimensions, flood plain status, ALR boundaries, easements and more. That is how I check whether a lot is really buildable, whether a property is in a flood zone, whether part of the backyard is a creek setback, or whether a “big lot” is mostly unbuildable. Below are the GIS tools I use most for BC properties, and how to use them yourself.

faq.q: Do I need GIS skills to buy a house?
faq.a: No. For a standard townhome or detached home in an established neighbourhood, GIS is rarely critical. It matters most when you are buying land, acreage, anything near water, anything in a flood zone, or anything you plan to build on, subdivide or significantly modify. For everything else, a quick check at the planning counter usually covers it.

faq.q: What is the difference between zoning and OCP?
faq.a: Zoning is the current rule: what you can build on the property today. The OCP (Official Community Plan) is what the city wants the area to become over the next 10 to 30 years. A property zoned single-family with a medium-density OCP designation is a redevelopment opportunity.

faq.q: How do I find out if a property is in a flood plain?
faq.a: Most municipal GIS maps have a flood plain layer you can switch on. Chilliwack MapOnline, Abbotsford CityMap and Delta’s map are the most relevant in this region, and BC iMap has provincial flood data. A flood plain does not stop you buying, but insurance, lending and rebuilding rules change, so know it before you write an offer.

faq.q: Can GIS tell me about easements and rights-of-way?
faq.a: Sometimes. GIS layers often show registered easements and obvious utility rights-of-way, but not every encumbrance shows on the map. Pull the title search for the full picture, and use GIS as a first look.
